attacks.claim: The plan makes a proprietary, closed-source, hosted-only SDK and server the single sync backend, directly contradicting the project's promise that users can self-host the sync server and own their data. Self-hosted users lose their sync path entirely in 5.0.
attacks.evidence: "the server component is available only as the hosted Cirrus Cloud service" and "Cirrus Cloud becomes the single sync backend and the stride-server Docker image is archived"

attacks.claim: Vendor lock-in with no exit plan: the client depends on a commercial binary SDK whose on-device store format and replication protocol are not documented, and the pricing tier is only 'free up to 100k MAU' with 90k users, leaving ~10% headroom and no cost ceiling for growth.
attacks.evidence: "Pricing: free up to 100k monthly active devices; our 90k fits the free tier." / "distributed as a prebuilt binary ... under the Cirrus commercial license"

attacks.claim: Shipping a MIT-licensed open-source app that depends on a closed commercial binary SDK and hosted-only server conflicts with the project's licensing and public charter promises; the plan does not assess license compatibility or ToS for redistribution.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any license compatibility analysis for the Cirrus commercial license versus the project's MIT license and charter

attacks.claim: The central claim that Cirrus resumable record-level uploads eliminate partial/duplicate workouts is unverified; the Week 1 spike occurs before any commitment yet the plan treats the approach as settled. No prototype or failure-injection test against the claim is referenced.
attacks.evidence: "uploads are resumable at the record level, so a dropped connection never leaves a partial workout." / ABSENT: prototype or test results validating this

attacks.claim: Health/location data (GPS tracks, workouts) is sent to a third-party hosted vendor, and account deletion relies on a vendor admin API with a 30-day window; no data processing agreement, residency, or verification of deletion from vendor backups is described.
attacks.evidence: "Account deletion removes the Cirrus user record and all synced records via the Cirrus admin API within 30 days."

attacks.claim: Archiving stride-server and removing legacy REST sync in 5.0 is a one-way door for ~3,000 self-hosted instances and their users' data; if Cirrus Cloud is discontinued, priced up, or fails, no fallback exists. Export is local-only, so migrating off Cirrus has no defined path.
attacks.evidence: "Legacy REST sync is removed in app 5.0 ... the stride-server Docker image is archived."

attacks.claim: The backup-and-rollback design is fragile: the backup is deleted after 30 days and two syncs, but a downgrade to 3.x after the Cirrus store has been written to and synced leaves the 3.x app restoring stale data, silently dropping post-migration workouts with no conflict path defined.
attacks.evidence: "If migration fails or the user downgrades to 3.x, 3.x detects stride-backup-v3.db and restores from it"

attacks.claim: Per-field LWW with on-device HLC cannot guarantee correctness with unsynchronized device clocks, and tombstones retained only 90 days allow an offline device (e.g. a trail runner out 3 months) to resurrect deleted workouts, contradicting the stated resurrection guarantee.
attacks.evidence: "Deletes are tombstones retained 90 days so an offline device cannot resurrect a deleted workout."

attacks.claim: Append-only-after-finish is undefined for workouts that are never explicitly finished (app killed, crash), leaving the lifecycle ambiguous for the conflict model.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: definition of the 'finish' event for crashed or abandoned workouts

attacks.claim: The 100k MAU free-tier ceiling is ~11% above current usage; growth of the app beyond that point, or counting of multi-device users, could trigger unplanned cost with no budget math given.
attacks.evidence: "free up to 100k monthly active devices; our 90k fits the free tier."

attacks.claim: No cost model exists for Cirrus beyond the free tier: storage, bandwidth for GPS tracks, and admin API usage are unquantified, and the plan commits to a vendor before cost is known.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: cost projection for GPS track sync volume and paid-tier pricing

attacks.claim: Rollout gate uses only crash-free sessions (99.3%) and does not gate on sync data loss or duplication, the exact problem being solved; a regression in data integrity could ship to 100% undetected.
attacks.evidence: "halting if crash-free sessions drop below 99.3%"

attacks.claim: No defined behavior when Cirrus Cloud is unreachable for extended periods or during vendor outage; no alerting or ops ownership for the hosted dependency is described.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: outage handling, alerting, and on-call ownership for Cirrus Cloud

attacks.claim: Plan does not address accessibility of migration/restore/sync-status UI shown to users during a multi-step migration and downgrade flow.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: accessibility requirements for migration and sync status UI

attacks.claim: The plan solves the trail-run loss problem by replacing the entire sync backend and forcing a vendor, while the stated problem (partial blob uploads) could plausibly be fixed with idempotent uploads on the existing protocol; the alternative is not evaluated.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: evaluation of alternatives such as idempotent or chunked uploads on the existing REST protocol

attacks.claim: Tests reference 14 scenarios in docs/sync-conflicts.md, which is not included in the artifact, so coverage cannot be verified; three contributors across a 5-week build with a proprietary SDK adds coupling risk.
attacks.evidence: "Unit tests cover the 14 conflict scenarios enumerated in docs/sync-conflicts.md."

attacks.claim: Plan does not describe authentication, token handling, or trust boundary for the Cirrus user record and admin API credentials used in account deletion.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: auth model and credential storage for Cirrus admin API

attacks.claim: Timeline is infeasible: a vendor integration spike, full migration with backup/restore, conflict resolution, a legacy path, beta, and staged rollout are compressed into 5 weeks for 3 contributors with no slack and no gate for the spike outcome.
attacks.evidence: "Week 1: Cirrus integration spike" through "Week 5: staged rollout"

attacks.claim: The plan replaces the self-hostable REST sync with a proprietary SDK whose server component exists only as hosted Cirrus Cloud, directly contradicting the charter's promise that users can self-host sync and own their data. Self-hosters (~3,000 instances) lose their sync backend when legacy REST is removed.
attacks.evidence: "the server component is available only as the hosted Cirrus Cloud service." and "Cirrus Cloud becomes the single sync backend and the stride-server Docker image is archived."

attacks.claim: Single-vendor lock-in with no documented exit path: the client is a closed binary under a commercial license, the server is hosted-only, and the plan has no migration or export-to-other-backend strategy if Cirrus pricing or terms change.
attacks.evidence: "distributed as a prebuilt binary (iOS xcframework, Android AAR) under the Cirrus commercial license"; ABSENT: any exit or alternative-backend plan

attacks.claim: Shipping a commercially licensed binary SDK into an MIT-licensed open-source project may conflict with the project's license and distribution terms, and the plan does not address license compatibility or redistribution rights.
attacks.evidence: "Stride is an open-source (MIT) running and workout tracker" vs "under the Cirrus commercial license"; ABSENT: license review

attacks.claim: The free-tier fit is asserted without verification of the pricing terms; '90k active users' is not the same as 'monthly active devices', and growth or multi-device users could exceed 100k and trigger cost.
attacks.evidence: "free up to 100k monthly active devices; our 90k fits the free tier."

attacks.claim: No cost model for paid tier overage, egress, or storage of GPS tracks in Cirrus Cloud; the plan has no budget ceiling for a vendor whose pricing may change.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: cost projections beyond the free-tier claim

attacks.claim: Workout data including GPS tracks (sensitive location data) will be replicated to a third-party cloud, but the plan says nothing about consent, data processing terms, retention, or residency for this data.
attacks.evidence: "Cirrus replicates to Cirrus Cloud when connectivity returns." and "GPS tracks" in schema mapping; ABSENT: privacy/consent review

attacks.claim: Account deletion depends on a third-party admin API completing within 30 days, with no verification or confirmation that vendor-side backups are purged.
attacks.evidence: "removes the Cirrus user record and all synced records via the Cirrus admin API within 30 days."

attacks.claim: Legacy REST sync removal and archiving the stride-server image is effectively a one-way door for self-hosters once 5.0 ships, with no stated rollback or migration tool for their data from self-hosted servers to Cirrus.
attacks.evidence: "Legacy REST sync is removed in app 5.0... the stride-server Docker image is archived."; ABSENT: self-host data migration path

attacks.claim: The 30-day backup retention and 'downgrade to 3.x' rollback rely on 3.x detecting stride-backup-v3.db, but a 4.x user who syncs to Cirrus and then downgrades may have writes that exist only in Cirrus, so rollback can silently lose or diverge data.
attacks.evidence: "If migration fails or the user downgrades to 3.x, 3.x detects stride-backup-v3.db and restores from it"

attacks.claim: The plan claims record-level resumability fixes partial uploads, but the 'finish' append-only model and per-field LWW on title/notes/gear are not shown to prevent duplicates when a record is partially synced, and no idempotency key is specified.
attacks.evidence: "uploads are resumable at the record level, so a dropped connection never leaves a partial workout." ABSENT: idempotency/dedup design

attacks.claim: Tombstones retained 90 days do not prevent resurrection for a device that stays offline longer than 90 days; the plan has no handling for that case, which would reintroduce deleted workouts.
attacks.evidence: "Deletes are tombstones retained 90 days so an offline device cannot resurrect a deleted workout."

attacks.claim: HLC is stamped on device, so clock skew or a manipulated device clock can make LWW pick the wrong winner; the plan does not describe clock-skew bounds or server-side ordering.
attacks.evidence: "per-field last-writer-wins using a hybrid logical clock stamped on device."

attacks.claim: Migration copies the full SQLite DB before migrating, which doubles local storage needs; no free-space check is specified, and a failed copy on a full device could corrupt the original.
attacks.evidence: "the app copies the existing SQLite database to stride-backup-v3.db before migrating"

attacks.claim: Migration of large histories in 500-workout chunks has no stated bound on total time or memory for users with many years of GPS-heavy data.
attacks.evidence: "Migration is chunked (500 workouts per batch)"

attacks.claim: Success metric of 80% reduction in lost/duplicated issues is set without a baseline measurement method, and the 23% figure is a share of sync issues, not a count of affected users.
attacks.evidence: "23% of sync-related GitHub issues in the last 6 months" and "down 80% within 2 months of 4.0."

attacks.claim: Rollout halt criterion depends only on crash-free sessions; there is no sync-correctness alert (duplicate or lost-workout detection) in the staged rollout, so silent data loss would not trigger a halt.
attacks.evidence: "halting if crash-free sessions drop below 99.3%."

attacks.claim: Timeline gives a 5-week build for SDK integration, migration, conflict resolution, a beta, and staged rollout across three contributors with no contingency.
attacks.evidence: "This plan is about to be dispatched to 3 contributors for a 5-week build."

attacks.claim: Legacy REST path is kept behind a flag while the Cirrus path is added, doubling the sync code surface during transition.
attacks.evidence: "legacy REST path behind custom-server flag."

attacks.claim: Plan says nothing about accessibility of migration prompts, failure messages, or backup/restore flows, which may be unusable for screen-reader users.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: accessibility review of migration and restore UI

attacks.claim: No UI copy or behavior is specified for the migration failure, downgrade, or 30-day backup deletion states, so users may see misleading or missing messages.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: UI spec for migration and backup states

attacks.claim: Migration is blocking on first launch with a full DB copy and chunked migration, with no stated progress or latency budget shown to the user.
attacks.evidence: "On first launch of 4.0, the app copies the existing SQLite database"

attacks.claim: The plan's own Problem section relies on a 'duplicate on re-upload' bug, but the proposed fix is a full vendor swap; the simpler option of fixing idempotency in the existing REST protocol is not evaluated, so the decision is not justified.

attacks.claim: The 3.x downgrade path restores from a local backup, but once a user syncs to Cirrus, a 3.x downgrade has no way to sync back; data diverges and the backup is deleted after 30 days, so post-migration writes can be lost on downgrade.
